<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="10" type="chapter">
                  <ns0:head>CHAP. X.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 AND the LORD said unto Moses, Go in unto Pharaoh: for <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 4. 21. and 7. 14.</ns0:note> I have hardned his heart, and the heart of his servants, that I might shew these my signs before him.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 And that <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 78. 5.</ns0:note> thou mayst tell in the ears of thy son, and of thy sons son, what things I have wrought in Egypt, and my signs which I have done amongst them: that ye may know how that I am the LORD.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 And Moses and Aaron came in unto Pharaoh, and said unto him, Thus saith the LORD God of the Hebrews, How long wilt thou refuse to hum<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ble thy self before me? Let my people go, that they may serve me.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 Else, if thou refuse to let my people go, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />hold, to morrow will I bring the <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Wisd. 16. 9.</ns0:note> locusts into thy coasts.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 And they shall cover the <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> eye.</ns0:note> face of the Earth, that one cannot be able to see the Earth, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Joel 1. 4.</ns0:note> they shall eat the residue of that which is escap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">The Wheat and the Rye, the staffe of their lives.</ns0:note>, which remaineth unto you from the hail, and shall eat every tree <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">The fruits and leaves of every tree.</ns0:note> which groweth for you out of the field.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 And they shall fill thy houses, and the houses of all thy servants, and the houses of all the Egyp<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tians, which neither thy fathers, nor thy fathers fathers have seen <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Such for number, or shape, or mischievous effects, as were never seen before.</ns0:note>, since the day that they were up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on the Earth unto this day. And he turned himself, and went out from Pharaoh.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 And Pharaohs servants said unto him, How long shall this man be a snare <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">An occasion of sin and destruction. See <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 23. 33. <ns0:hi>Ios.</ns0:hi> 23. 1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> unto us? let the men go, that they may serve the LORD their God: knowest thou not yet, that Egypt is de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stroyed?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:57" />
                  <ns0:gap reason="duplicate" extent="1 page">
                     <ns0:desc>〈1 page duplicate〉</ns0:desc>
                  </ns0:gap>
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:57" />
                  <ns0:gap reason="duplicate" extent="1 page">
                     <ns0:desc>〈1 page duplicate〉</ns0:desc>
                  </ns0:gap>
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:58" />
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 And Moses and Aaron were brought again unto Pharaoh: and he said unto them, Go serve the LORD your God: <ns0:hi>but</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>who and who,</ns0:hi> &c.</ns0:note> who <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> they that shall go?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 And Moses said, We will go with our young, and with our old, with our sons, and with our daughters, with our flocks, and with our herds will we go, for we <ns0:hi>must bold</ns0:hi> a feast unto the LORD <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">A feast upon a sacrifice, wherein all are concerned, and therefore all must be present and ready to do what God re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quires us.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 And he said unto them, Let the LORD be so with you, as I will let you go <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">I wish God may be no more ready and willing to be with you and to do you good than I am willing to let you go.</ns0:note>, and your little ones. Look to it, for evil is before you <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Ei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther 1. Evil of sin. You have some ill design against me, either to stir up Sedition or War against me, or utterly to depart out of my Kingdom. Or rather 2. Evil of calamity or mischief. 1. Because it is here said to be <ns0:hi>before</ns0:hi> their <ns0:hi>faces,</ns0:hi> whereas evil de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />signs are in mens hearts, and the fair pretences wherewith they cover them are said to be before their faces. 2. The word of caution he gives to them, <ns0:hi>look to it</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>take <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>eed,</ns0:hi> seems to imply that he speaks not of the evil they designed against <ns0:hi>Pharaoh,</ns0:hi> but of that which they would unavoidably bring upon themselves from so potent a King, by the refusal of such fair offers and continuing in such insolent and unreasonable demands.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 Not so: go now ye <ns0:hi>that are</ns0:hi> men and serve the LORD, for that ye did desire <ns0:note n="†" place="bottom">Which was not true, but onely was gathered by him out of their declared intention of going to sacrifice, wherein he thought the presence of the Women and Children wholly un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />necessary.</ns0:note>: and they were driven out from Pharaohs presence.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 And the LORD said unto Moses, stretch out thine hand over the land of Egypt for the lo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />custs, that they may come up upon the land of Egypt, and eat every herb of the land <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">This is no unusual Plague in <ns0:hi>Africa</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Arabia,</ns0:hi> where, when the harvest is ripe, they frequently come in vast numbers and eat up all their Corn, and what they do not eat they infect with their touch and the moisture coming from them, and after<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />wards dying in great numbers they poison the Air and cause a pestilence. So that it is no wonder that <ns0:hi>Pharaoh</ns0:hi> and his Ser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vants were so concerned for this Plague, so well known to them, especially considering, that this was like to be far worse then all of the same kind which they had either seen or heard of.</ns0:note>, even all that the hail hath left.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 And Moses stretched forth his rod over the land <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Over divers parts of the Land, shaking his rod towards the several quarters of it.</ns0:note> of Egypt, and the LORD brought an East<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />wind <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Which in those parts is a most vio<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lent and pernicious wind, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 14. 21. <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 11. 31. and a dry wind, and therefore fit for the ingendring of those Creatures. This wind brought them from <ns0:hi>Arabia,</ns0:hi> where they are in great numbers, as we have seen <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 12. though God miraculously in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />creased their numbers and their power of doing mischief.</ns0:note> upon the land, all that day, and all that night, and when it was morning, the East-wind brought the locusts.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14 And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 78. 46. and 105. 34.</ns0:note> the locusts went up over all the land of Egypt, and rested in all the coasts of E<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gypt: very grievous were they: before them there were no such locusts as they, neither after them shall be such <ns0:note n="†" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Quest.</ns0:hi> How can this be true, when the same words are used of the locusts in <ns0:hi>Ioe<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>s</ns0:hi> time? <ns0:hi>Answ.</ns0:hi> It might be true of both in divers respects, of these for number and quality, of them for long continuance, for they lasted three or four years, when these were but for a little time; of these for <ns0:hi>Egypt,</ns0:hi> of them for <ns0:hi>Iud<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>a,</ns0:hi> where they were fixed.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15 For they covered the face of the whole earth, so that the land was darkned <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Either by their flying in vast numbers and so darkning the air, as they have oft times done: or by covering the green and lightsome herbs and productions of the earth with their dark and direful bodies.</ns0:note>, and they did eat every herb of the land, and all the fruit of the trees, which the hail had left <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">How could this be, when the hail had <ns0:hi>smitten every herb, and broken every tree, chap.</ns0:hi> 9. 25. <ns0:hi>Ans.</ns0:hi> 1. There seems to have been some distance of time between these two plagues, in which space, new productions might be sprouting forth both out of the ground and from the trees. 2. The words <ns0:hi>all</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>every</ns0:hi> are commonly understood of the greatest part.</ns0:note>, and there remained not any green thing in the trees, or in the herbs of the field, through all the land of Egypt.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16 Then Pharaoh <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> hastned to call.</ns0:note> called for Moses and Aa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ron in haste <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Because this kind of plague in it self was most pernicious, whereby whole countries had been wasted and grievous fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mines and pestilences caused, and was mightily aggravated by the vengeance of God and by the peculiar quality of these Lo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />custs, which did not onely fall upon their herbs and fruits, as they use to do, but invade their very houses, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 6. infect their meats, fill their beds, poison them with their stink and with their venemous bitings, whereby they killed many men, as it is written in the book of <ns0:hi>Wisdom,</ns0:hi> chap. 16. <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 19.</ns0:note>: and he said, I have sinned against the LORD your God, and against you <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">By contempt of your great and terrible works, by breach of my promise made to you, and by my denial of your just desires and commands given to me in his name whom I now find and feel to be the almighty and soveraign God.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17 Now therefore forgive, I pray thee, my sin only this once <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">I desire no further favour, I will no more offend nor need your pardon.</ns0:note>, and intreat the LORD your God, that he may take away from me this death <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">This deadly plague, compare 2 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 4. 40. and 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 11. 23. Besides it did destroy the life of herbs and trees, yea of beasts and men, either directly, or at least by consequence in depriving them of the necessary sup<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ports of life.</ns0:note> only.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18 And he went out from Pharaoh, and in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />treated the LORD.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19 And the LORD turned a mighty strong West-wind <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>a wind of the Sea, i. e.</ns0:hi> coming from the Sea, called there the great Sea, and the <ns0:hi>Mediterranean</ns0:hi> Sea, from whence came the North-west wind, which did blow the locusts di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rectly into the Red-sea.</ns0:note>, which took away the locusts, and <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> fastned.</ns0:note> cast them <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Cast them,</ns0:hi> as the <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> word signi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fies, <ns0:hi>with a great noise, and with great force,</ns0:hi> so as they should never rise again to molest them.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Joel. 2. 20.</ns0:note> into the Red-sea <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>the sea of bulrushes,</ns0:hi> so called from the great number of bulrushes near its shore, Or, <ns0:hi>the sea of bounds</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>limits, q. d.</ns0:hi> the narrow sea, whereas they could see no bounds nor shore beyond the <ns0:hi>Mediterranean</ns0:hi> Sea. It was cal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />led the <ns0:hi>Arabian</ns0:hi> gulf, and by others the <ns0:hi>Red-sea,</ns0:hi> either from its red sand; or rather from <ns0:hi>Esau,</ns0:hi> called also <ns0:hi>Edom,</ns0:hi> which signi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fies <ns0:hi>red, Gen.</ns0:hi> 25. 30. from whom as the adjoyning country was called <ns0:hi>Edom,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>red,</ns0:hi> so this was called the <ns0:hi>Red-sea.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>: there re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mained not one locust in all the coasts of Egypt.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">20 But the LORD <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 4. 21.</ns0:note> hardened Pharaohs heart, so that he would not let the children of Israel go.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21 And the LORD said unto Moses, Stretch out thine hand toward heaven, that there may be darkness over the land of Egypt, <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> that one may feel darkness</ns0:note> even dark<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness which may be felt <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">It is an hyperbolical expression, such being very frequent both in Scripture and in all authors. For darkness being onely a privation cannot be properly felt, yet it might be felt in its cause, to wit, those thick and gross vapours which filled and in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fected the Air. But the place may be rendred thus, <ns0:hi>that there may be darkness—after that</ns0:hi> (so the Hebrew <ns0:hi>Va<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>
                        </ns0:hi> is some<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />times used, as <ns0:hi>Micb.</ns0:hi> 7. 13.) <ns0:hi>the darkness (i. e. the darkness</ns0:hi> of the night, or the common and daily <ns0:hi>darkness) is departed</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />moved,</ns0:hi> and the time of the day come: for so the root, from whence this word may be derived, signifies, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 13. 22. And to this purpose the words are rendred by the <ns0:hi>Chaldee</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Syriack,</ns0:hi> and some others, and the sence is, that the darkness may continue in the day-time as well as in the night.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="22">22 And Moses stretched forth his hand toward heaven: and there was a <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 105. 28.</ns0:note> thick darkness in all the land of Egypt three dayes.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="23">23 They saw not one another <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Because these gross and moist fogs and vapours did not onely quite shut out the light of the heavenly bodies, but also put out their candles or other artificial lights, or at least so darken them that men could have no benefit by them.</ns0:note>, neither rose any from his place <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Place</ns0:hi> here may be taken, either <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>1. more strictly and particularly: so the sence is, the horrour of that darkness was so great that they durst not remove at all, but stood or sat where the darkness found them, like men astonished or affrighted, and therefore unmoveable, having their minds disturbed, being terrified with their guilty Consciences, which most affect men in the dark, and with the dreadful noises which they heard, <ns0:hi>Wisd.</ns0:hi> 17. 5. and with the apparitions of evil Angels, as may seem from <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 78. 49. where the plague of evil Angels is put instead of this plague of darkness, which therefore is omit<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ted in that place where all the rest are reckoned up. Or ra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther 2. more largely, for their own houses or dwellings, for so the Hebrew word is certainly used, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 16. 29. So the sence is, they did not stir abroad out of their houses upon their most necessary occasions. <ns0:hi>Obj.</ns0:hi> He saith not that they could not go, but that they could not <ns0:hi>rise</ns0:hi> from their place, which may seem to limit this expression to their particular places. <ns0:hi>Ans.</ns0:hi> The word, <ns0:hi>to rise,</ns0:hi> is commonly put for going about any business, and here it is a pregnant word, as they call it, and implies going in it, <ns0:hi>none arose,</ns0:hi> viz. to go or remove, <ns0:hi>from his place.</ns0:hi> And <ns0:hi>rising</ns0:hi> cannot be properly taken here for that particular posture, unless we will suppose that this darkness found all men sitting, which is absurd to imagine.</ns0:note> for three dayes: <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Wisd. 18. 1. chap. 8. 22.</ns0:note> but all the children of Israel had light in their dwel<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lings <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Whereby they might have conveyed themselves and families and goods away, as afterwards they did in haste: but they waited for <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> his orders, and he for Gods command, and God intended to bring them forth not by stealth, but in a more honourable and publick manner, in spight of all opposition.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="24">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:58" />24 And <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>Therefore:</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Then,</ns0:hi> to wit, after the darkness was either wholly or in part removed.</ns0:note> Pharaoh called unto Moses, and said, Go ye, serve the LORD: only let your flocks and your herds be stayed <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Either as a pledge of your return after your sacrifice is ended: or as a recompence for the cattel which I have lost by your means.</ns0:note>: let your little ones <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">And consequently the women, whose help and service was necessary for their little ones in diverse regards.</ns0:note> al<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />so go with you.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="25">25 And Moses said, Thou must give <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> into our hands.</ns0:note> us <ns0:note n="*" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Suffer us to take of our own stock.</ns0:note> al<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />so sacrifices, and burnt-offerings, that we may sacrifice unto the LORD our God.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="26">26 Our cattel also shall go with us, there shall not an hoof be left behind, for thereof must we take to serve the LORD our God: and we know not with what we must serve the LORD until we come thither <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Which was not a pretence, but a real truth. For this being a solemn and extraordinary sacrifice by the express and particular appointment of God, they knew not either of what kinds, or in what number or manner their sacrifices must be offered. And for all these things they did not receive par<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ticular directions till they came to mount <ns0:hi>Sinai.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="27">27 But the LORD <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 14. 4, 8.</ns0:note> hardened Pharaohs heart, and he would not let them go.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="28">28 And Pharaoh said unto him, Get thee from me, take heed to thy self: see my face no more: for in that day thou seest my face, thou shalt die.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="29">29 And Moses said, thou hast spoken well <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>right,</ns0:hi> not morally, for so it was very ill said; but logically, that which agrees though not with thy duty, yet with the event and truth of the thing: for as thou hast warned me to see thee no more, so I in the name of God assure thee, that thou shalt see me no more, to beg my prayers, or to be helped out of thy troubles by my means. And therefore that discourse of <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> to <ns0:hi>Pharaoh,</ns0:hi> which follows <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 11. 4, &c. though it be put there out of its order and proper place, as many other passages are, yet was delivered at this time and upon occasion of these words.</ns0:note>, I will see thy face again no more.</ns0:p>
